q: According to R. Zeira, why do Beit Shammai require a dinar for betrothal?
options: A woman is particular about her dignity and won't accept less
A dinar is the smallest Tyrian coin
The *amah ivriyah* deducts from her price
why: *Makpedet al atzmah*. He limits it to a betrothal at night or through an agent, where she couldn't see the amount.

q: Abaye asks about R. Yannai's daughters, who would insist on much more. What if one of them reaches out and accepts a single dinar?
options: She is betrothed: she may give up her own dignity
She is betrothed only with three *kav* of dinars
why: R. Zeira's rule applies only where she couldn't see what she received.

options: Tyrian coinage, used for sums set in the Torah
Provincial coinage, about one-eighth the value
why: For Rav Asi, Torah sums are in Tyrian coin; sums set by the Sages are in *kesef medinah*.

q: How is Rav Asi's rule finally restated?
options: Only a set sum (*kesef katzuv*) in the Torah is Tyrian
All 'money' in the Torah is Tyrian
why: Where the Torah simply says 'money', any coin works, even copper; where it names a number, the Tyrian coin is meant.

q: In which coinage are the fifty *sela* paid by a rapist or seducer?
why: A sum set by the Torah. The one-*sela* fine for an insulting blow, set by the Sages, is provincial: half a dinar.

q: Why may second-tithe money be exchanged even for copper coins?
options: '*The* money' amplifies to include any coinage
why: The definite article in Devarim 14:25 widens it beyond Tyrian silver.

q: How does R. Shimon ben Lakish explain Beit Shammai's dinar?
options: From the *amah ivriyah*, who deducts from her price, impossible from a *perutah*
why: *Megara'at ve'yotzet*: a price of one *perutah* leaves nothing to deduct.
